item.title: Temporal characteristics-based urban heat island effect assessment
item.description:
Urban heat island effect (UHIE) assessments support heat reduction and climate-responsive strategies by informing urban planners, urban designers and local city administrations. Conventional UHIE assessments commonly rely on satellite-derived land surface temperature (LST) to identify hotspots, implicitly treating these locations as thermally representative across intra-day observation periods and seasons. To evaluate this assumption, the temporal characteristics of LST-identified hotspots across the Chennai Metropolitan Area of Tamil Nadu, India, were assessed using one year of field-based air-temperature observations collected from 100 locations representing heterogeneous urban morphology. The assessment analysed thermal hierarchy, thermal-state transitions, persistence and long-term rankings. The results reveal substantial intra-day variability in localised UHIE. The relative thermal hierarchy changed across the morning, afternoon and evening observation periods. Nearly all locations exhibited volatility in their thermal state in at least 25% of observations, while 25% exhibited volatility in more than 50% of observations. Long-term hotspot rankings derived from LST, air temperature and thermal persistence showed limited agreement. More than one-third (36%) of locations identified as hotspots by mean daytime LST were not identified by any other indicator. These findings demonstrate that thermal persistence constitutes an essential dimension of UHIE assessment which supports a more dynamic understanding beyond static LST-based hotspot mapping.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

In 2019, under Section 18(2) of the Disaster Management Act, 2005, of the Government of India, the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) laid down guidance on prevention, mitigation and preparedness for heatwaves. As part of this framework, local city administrations are requested by the NDMA to prepare ‘heat action plans’ (HAPs). The UHIE assessment forms an integral component of these HAPs. Current UHIE assessments primarily rely on satellite-derived LST-based hotspot identification. This approach does not capture the temporal characteristics of localised UHIE. This study demonstrates that incorporating thermal persistence alongside conventional thermal indicators enables practitioners to distinguish persistently hot locations from transient hotspots. This additional temporal dimension can strengthen the prioritisation of heat-mitigation interventions and support more targeted investigation of the factors contributing to localised heat stress in rapidly urbanising cities.

item.title: Uncertainty and equivocality in reuse-oriented deconstruction
item.description:
Deconstruction aimed at element reuse is recognised as a circular practice, yet it remains a particularly challenging alternative to conventional demolition. To better understand these challenges, this study adopts an information-processing perspective that frames reuse challenges as rooted in both uncertainty and equivocality. While uncertainty arises from missing or incomplete information, equivocality stems from multiple, sometimes conflicting, interpretations of the same information. Drawing on empirical data from four Dutch reuse-oriented projects, this study develops a conceptual framework mapping building, workflow, and environmental uncertainty and equivocality. The findings also suggest that some forms of project-level equivocality in deconstruction may be linked to unresolved uncertainties at the sector level. As these challenges extend beyond individual projects, addressing them may require institutional learning and sector-wide coordination. These findings extend existing information-processing theory by suggesting that sectoral uncertainty-reducing mechanisms, including standardised reusability guidelines, formalised responsibility structures and regulatory frameworks tailored to deconstruction, may also mitigate project-level equivocality by narrowing the space of plausible interpretations.

PRACTICE RELEVANCE

Actionable insights are provided for demolition contractors navigating the information-processing challenges of reuse-oriented deconstruction. By distinguishing uncertainty from equivocality, the findings clarify which challenges require the collection of new information and which require interpretive alignment among stakeholders—a distinction with direct implications for how contractors select and deploy coordination mechanisms. Both established and deconstruction-specific mechanisms are identified that practitioners can tailor to their project contexts. The limitations of organisational responses at the project level point to a further need for coordinated action from policymakers and industry bodies to develop shared standards and regulatory frameworks that support reuse. Without such sector-wide coordination, reuse may remain a coordination-intensive exception rather than a scalable practice.

item.title: Modern methods of construction and the future of housing
item.description: Housing faces intersecting crises of affordability, supply and decarbonisation, and modern methods of construction (MMC) are increasingly promoted to transform both new build and retrofit. This editorial introduces a special issue that explores the political, social and cultural implications of MMC for housing. Seven articles apply critical social science perspectives to MMC housing in the UK, Germany, Estonia, Vietnam, Malaysia, Australia and the US. Moving beyond techno-optimistic and productivity-based narratives, the contributions examine policy roadmaps, political economy and multilevel governance aspects of systemic change, innovation systems and institutional readiness, systemic intermediaries, and residents’ everyday experiences. Interrogating some of the claims made about the transformative potential of MMC, together they show that MMC offers tangible benefits, including speed, quality and reduced disruption, but that these are neither guaranteed nor evenly distributed. Its prospects depend less on technological innovation than on systemic coordination, stable long-term demand, place-based conditions and outcome-focused public policy. Future avenues for research are highlighted: comparative and longitudinal studies, whole-life verification of claimed benefits, greater attention to liveability and the experiences of residents and tenants, distributional and workforce effects, and the scaling of MMC in retrofit.
